title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
question: Can a steering vector built from contrastive multiple-choice answer pairs, added to the residual stream at inference, shift Llama 2 Chat behaviour on alignment-relevant traits?
mechanism: For a chosen layer L, run each contrast pair (same question; one prompt ends with the behaviour-positive answer letter, the other with the behaviour-negative letter) and record residual-stream activations at the answer-letter token. Steering vector = mean over pairs of (a_L(positive) - a_L(negative)). At inference, add multiplier x vector to the residual stream at all token positions after the user instruction (multipliers 2 and -2 in the sycophancy example, Table 1). Layer chosen by sweep.
training: none for the vector: forward passes over contrast pairs and a mean difference, no gradient training. The packet gives no pair count beyond 'hundreds of diverse contrast pairs'.
setup: Llama 2 7B Chat and 13B Chat (base 7B used for vector similarity/transfer); behaviours include coordination with other AIs, corrigibility, hallucination, myopic reward, survival instinct, sycophancy and refusal; multiple-choice behavioural evals and GPT-4-rated open-ended generation on a 1-10 scale.
numbers: Section 4 (qualitative result as stated in text; Tables 3 and 4 cells not transcribed): 'Adding the steering vector increases the behavioral evaluation score beyond just using a positive system prompt and vice versa for subtracting the steering vector.'
Section 4 (Table 3 text): 'As shown in Table 3, for most behaviors tested, CAA can modify model behavior beyond what is achieved through prompting alone.' (table values not extracted).
limits: Steering with larger multipliers degrades the quality of open-ended text, per the authors' multiplier exploration (Section 4).
evidence_quote: prompts designed to elicit the behavior or its opposite. Steering is performed at layer 13.

title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
question: Is refusal in chat models mediated by a single one-dimensional direction in the residual stream, and can that direction be removed by a simple weight edit?
mechanism: Difference-in-means direction r^(l) = mean activation on harmful instructions minus mean on harmless instructions, per layer l and post-instruction token position; one candidate (layer, position) is selected on validation prompts by bypassing refusal when ablated and inducing refusal when added. Inference-time directional ablation removes the r_hat component from every residual-stream activation. Weight orthogonalization (Sec 4.1): for each matrix W_out that writes to the residual stream (embedding, positional embedding, attention out, MLP out, and output biases), W_out <- W_out - r_hat r_hat^T W_out, so the model never writes r_hat to the stream; the paper states this is equivalent to the inference-time ablation.
training: none: the direction is a difference of means over 128 harmful and 128 harmless training instructions (32+32 validation prompts for candidate selection); the weight edit needs no gradient-based optimisation and no harmful completions (Sec 4).
setup: 13 open chat models from 1.8B to 72B (Qwen Chat, Yi Chat, Gemma IT, Llama-2 Chat, Llama-3 Instruct); harmful training sets from AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct, TDC2023 and HarmBench; harmless from Alpaca; evaluation on 100 JailbreakBench harmful instructions and HarmBench ASR.
numbers: Figure 1 (intro): ablating the refusal direction reduces refusal rates and elicits unsafe completions across the 13 models (per-model scores are in the figure, not transcribed).

Sec 4 (weight orthogonalization): the orthogonalized model 'retains its original capabilities but no longer refuses harmful instructions' (qualitative); Table 2 gives ASR against HarmBench comparators (cells not transcribed).
Sec 4 (Table 3): on MMLU, ARC and GSM8K, orthogonalized models 'perform similarly' to the originals (cells not transcribed).
limits: Covers 13 open chat models; the paper reports the weight edit as equivalent to inference-time directional ablation, so its effect is no broader than the ablation (Sec 4.1).
The mechanism for adversarial suffixes is described as preliminary (intro).
evidence_quote: We then use this insight to design a simple white-box jailbreak via an interpretable rank-one weight edit that effectively disables refusal with minimal impact on other capabilities

novelty_note.A: Rank-one weight edit that orthogonalises every residual-stream-writing matrix to the difference-in-means refusal direction r_hat; the direction is computed in closed form from forward passes over harmful and harmless prompts, and the edit changes a behaviour (refusal), not a single fact.

title: Analysing the Generalisation and Reliability of Steering Vectors
question: How reliable and how generalisable are CAA steering vectors, per input and under changes to the system or user prompt?
mechanism: CAA: steering vector v_MD = mean over training triples of (a_L(x,y+) - a_L(x,y-)), residual-stream activations at the answer-option token; applied as lambda * v_L added at the last token position at layer L during inference, lambda a multiplier. Per-input steerability: Delta mLD(x) = mLD_steered(x) - mLD_not_steered(x), with logit-difference propensity mLD = logit(y+) - logit(y-); an input is anti-steerable when Delta mLD < 0. Out-of-distribution test: injects prompt text into the system or user message to elicit more or less of the behaviour, then applies the vector trained on the default prompt.
training: none: mean-difference extraction over contrast pairs, no gradient training; layer and multiplier chosen on a validation split.
setup: Model-Written Evals (MWE) datasets: 40 datasets including TruthfulQA and sycophancy, 40-10-50 train/val/test split per dataset; several models for the cross-model comparison; A100 40 GB (Appendix A).
numbers: Figure 1 caption: 'several datasets produce the opposite behaviour for almost 50% of inputs' (per-sample steerability shown for 13 of 40 datasets).
Abstract: steerability 'is highly variable across different inputs'; 'for several concepts they are brittle to reasonable changes in the prompt'.
Results (in-distribution section, full text): 'Many of these datasets have almost half of the inputs being anti-steerable'.
limits: Many datasets have a large fraction of anti-steerable inputs, so aggregate effects can overstate reliability (intro).
Out-of-distribution steering is brittle for several concepts; generalisation is not perfect or entirely predictable (intro).
evidence_quote: Depending on the concept, spurious biases can substantially contribute to how effective steering is for each input, presenting a challenge for the widespread use of steering vectors.

novelty_note.G: Reports a 'steerability bias' in which models are easier to steer toward outputs with a property such as answer position or token choice (Figure 3), so the steering effect can reflect the prompt template rather than the intended concept.

title: Refusal in LLMs is an Affine Function
question: Does steering refusal with an affine concept edit, rather than a linear one, give more standardised and reliable control than CAA or directional ablation?
mechanism: Affine concept editing (ACE): v' = v - proj_r^parallel(v) + alpha0 r + alpha r. r is the concept direction (difference of positive and negative class means); alpha0 r = proj_r^parallel(v0) is a reference offset chosen so that alpha = 0 maps to the null-behaviour mean and alpha = 1 to the behaviour mean; alpha is the new coefficient. It combines removing the existing component along r (directional ablation) with adding back the chosen offset (CAA).
training: none in the packet: the direction and offset are computed from class means over prompt sets.
setup: Ten chat models including Llama 3 70B for refusal control; an RWKV v5 recurrent model (Hermes Eagle); LLM-based scoring on harmful and harmless prompts.
numbers: Abstract: ACE 'consistently achieves more precise control over model behavior than existing methods' and 'generalizes to models where directional ablation via affine subspace projection alone produces incoherent outputs' (quantitative tables not captured in packet).
limits: Directional ablation alone produces incoherent outputs on some models (Hermes Eagle RWKV v5) (Sec 2.2).
evidence_quote: ACE combines affine subspace projection and activation addition to reliably control the model’s refusal responses across prompt types.

title: AxBench: Steering LLMs? Even Simple Baselines Outperform Sparse Autoencoders
question: Which concept-control methods (prompting, finetuning, SAEs, difference-in-means, a new rank-1 ReFT method) perform best on open-vocabulary concept detection and long-form steering?
mechanism: Benchmark: an LLM generates labelled data for each concept description (500 concepts per task). Positives are responses that incorporate the concept; negatives are unsteered responses to instructions from all genres; hard negatives are semantically related concepts (evaluation only). Steering methods compared include difference-in-means (DiffMean) added to the residual stream, SAE feature clamping, prompting, full finetuning, LoRA, LoReFT, and ReFT-r1, a new weakly supervised rank-1 representation finetuning. Steered outputs are rated by an LLM judge.
training: Mixed: DiffMean, SAE and prompting need no gradient training; finetuning, LoRA, LoReFT and ReFT-r1 are gradient-trained. Main experiments use n = 144 training examples per concept (Sec 3.1).
setup: Instruction-tuned Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B; eight tasks (4 representation sites x 2 axes: concept detection and model steering) using GemmaScope SAE concept lists; training and evaluation data generated with gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18.
numbers: Abstract: 'For steering, we find that prompting outperforms all existing methods, followed by finetuning.' (ranking only; per-method scores are in Figure 1, not transcribed).
Sec 3.1: 'We set n = 144 for our main experiments.' (training examples per concept).
limits: The authors say representation steering methods 'largely lag behind incumbent model-control techniques' on steering, and that SAEs fall behind both ReFT-r1 and difference-in-means on both axes (intro).

title: Understanding (Un)Reliability of Steering Vectors in Language Models
venue: ICLR 2025 Workshop on Foundation Models in the Wild (per header)
question: How do the prompt types used to generate steering-vector training activations, and the geometry of the activation differences, predict whether CAA steering is reliable?
mechanism: CAA: steering vector s_l = mean over training triples of (a_l(x,y+) - a_l(x,y-)) at the answer-token position, added as lambda * s_l to the residual stream at layer l (lambda = 1 in most experiments). Seven prompt types vary whether the answer token is prefilled, whether an instruction encouraging or discouraging the behaviour is prepended, and whether 5-shot examples are included; these change the activations from which the vector is built. Predictors: directional agreement (cosine between each training activation difference and the steering vector) and separability (discriminability along the difference-of-means line).
training: none: mean difference over 250 training samples per dataset and prompt type; no gradient training.
setup: Llama2-7B-chat; 36 binary-choice datasets from Rogers et al. (2023) on assistant personality and behaviour; layer 13; 500 evaluation prompts per dataset with logit-difference propensity.
numbers: Section 3: 'The fraction of such anti-steerable samples ranges from 3% to 50% for individual datasets.'
Section 3: vectors trained on the same samples with different prompts have 'pairwise cosine similarities ranging from 0.07 to 0.86'.
Figure 1 (top row, 'Most steerable datasets (group 1-6)'): mean effect 2.74 with 17.5% anti-steerable samples; the prompt type this row refers to is not resolved from the packet.
limits: Steering is unreliable when the target behaviour is not represented by a coherent direction (abstract).
interp: different prompt types give directionally distinct vectors with similar efficacy, so the vector is not a stable object across extraction choices.
evidence_quote: a representative steering method where the steering vector is computed as the mean difference between activations of datapoints with and without the desired behavior

novelty_note.D: Prepended instructions (encouraging or discouraging the behaviour) and 5-shot examples are used to generate the positive and negative activations from which the steering vector is built, so an instruction is converted into an activation direction.

title: Scaling laws for activation steering with Llama 2 models and refusal mechanisms
venue: Accepted at NewInML workshop, ICML 2025 (per header)
question: How does CAA steering effectiveness on refusal change with Llama 2 model size (7B, 13B, 70B) and with layer?
mechanism: CAA on a refusal answer-matching dataset: cache last-token residual-stream vectors at every layer for positive (refusal) and negative examples; per layer, average the pairwise difference vectors and normalise the mean to the average norm of the differences; add this vector at every token position just before the add-and-normalise step after the MLP of that layer, which preserves residual norms; sweep all layers and measure the change in probability of the correct refusal behaviour.
training: none: forward passes and averaging only, no gradient training.
setup: Llama 2 7B, 13B and 70B (chat models); refusal answer-matching dataset.
numbers: Section 4: 'Steering efficacy peaks in early-mid layers, at approximately 0.4 × total layer count.'
Section 4 exponential fit, as written: y = 0.081 + 2.4 · e−0.42·x, with y the peak effectiveness and x the parameter count (units of x not stated in packet).
Section 4: peak positive and negative steering layers converge with size (7B: 2-layer difference, 13B: 1 layer, 70B: 0 layers).
limits: Experiments limited to refusal; the authors say further experiments with a more complete set of behaviours are needed (Sec 4).
Negative (toward non-refusal) steering is more effective than positive steering at all three sizes; the authors hypothesise this comes from RLHF (Sec 4).
evidence_quote: Lastly, we average these direction vectors for each layer and normalize its magnitude to the average norm of these direction vectors across our dataset.

title: Mechanistic Indicators of Steering Effectiveness in Large Language Models
question: Can the success of activation steering (CAA, SAE steering) be predicted from internal signals, namely normalised branching factor (entropy) and KL divergence against concept vocabularies?
mechanism: Normalised Branching Factor: B_t = exp(H(p_t^eff)), the exponential of the entropy of the next-token distribution restricted to an effective vocabulary of the N most probable tokens. KL features: divergence between steered and unsteered output distributions over behaviour- or concept-specific vocabularies. Summary statistics (mean, median, range, skewness, kurtosis, variance, std, min, max) of these signals at generation step t = 30 are standard-scaled and fed to a feed-forward regressor that predicts an LLM-judge steering score; the judge annotations are treated as ground truth.
training: Supervised: the regression model (FNN) is gradient-trained on LLM-judge annotations of steering outcomes; the packet gives 2,304 steering experiments in total (regression-split details not in packet). The steering itself is training-free.
setup: Gemma 2 2B for the worked examples (London concept; rotational and additive steering functions; CAA and SAE extraction); two LLM judges (ChatGPT-4o-mini and Gemini-Flash-2.5); five random seeds for the regressor.
numbers: Table 1 (regression): R2 = 0.4698 ± 0.0022 with ChatGPT-4o-mini annotations; R2 = 0.5445 ± 0.0012 with Gemini-Flash-2.5 annotations.
Contributions item 1: 'steering ... (2,304 experiments)' used to test LLM judges as annotators.
limits: interp: the reliability study compares two LLM judges only, so judge bias shared by both is not tested.
Qualitative examples are cherry-picked, per the authors (contributions item 2).

title: On the Non-Identifiability of Steering Vectors in Large Language Models
question: Is a steering vector uniquely recoverable from behaviour, or do large equivalence classes of behaviourally indistinguishable vectors exist?
mechanism: Local linearisation: o(x,v,alpha) ≈ o(x,0,0) + alpha J_l(x) v, with J_l the Jacobian of output logits with respect to the hidden state at layer l. Any perturbation v_perp in ker(J) leaves the first-order output unchanged. The null-space dimension is estimated by SVD of the activation covariance matrix over the same contrast pairs; equivalence is tested by adding orthogonal perturbations to a steering vector and comparing effect sizes (Cohen's d) using a pre-trained semantic classifier and raw logits.
training: none for the steering vectors (CAA and other extraction methods); the study is analytic plus forward-pass experiments.
setup: Two model families at mid-network layers, five semantic traits; extraction methods including contrastive and PCA vectors; several prompt distributions.
numbers: Results (equivalence paragraph, full text): cosine similarities between the two vectors 'range from −0.54 to +0.32', while 'Cohen's d remains below 0.27 in all conditions'.
Results (ten-seed check, full text): 'mean Cohen's d is 0.119 for Llama and 0.131 for Qwen, well below the negligible-effect threshold'.
limits: Empirical validation covers two models at mid-network layers across five traits; magnitude may vary by model family, scale and layer (Limitations).
The authors do not verify that the SVD-estimated semantic null space coincides with the Jacobian null space (Limitations).
evidence_quote: Empirically, we find that orthogonal perturbations achieve near-equivalent efficacy with negligible effect sizes across multiple models and traits

novelty_note.G: Shows that orthogonal perturbations to a steering vector, which leave the logits unchanged to first order, produce the same behavioural effect, so 'the observed behavioral effect of steering does not localize semantic content to a specific direction' (paper's wording).

title: Endogenous Resistance to Activation Steering in Language Models
venue: Proceedings of the 43rd ICML, PMLR 306, 2026 (per header)
question: When an SAE-latent steering vector pushes a model off topic, do models recover mid-generation with explicit self-correction, and what drives that recovery?
mechanism: SAE steering: boost one SAE latent (GemmaScope or Goodfire SAEs) on every generated token by an additive intervention of chosen strength. Explicit endogenous steering resistance (ESR) is scored by a judge (Claude 4.5 Haiku) that segments the response into attempts at explicit self-correction phrases and scores each attempt 0-100 for relevance to the prompt while avoiding the steering topic. Mechanism search: contrastive on-topic/off-topic search over SAE latents, then zero-ablation; controls use random latents and held-out prompts.
training: Steering is training-free; a separate experiment fine-tunes Llama-3.1-8B on synthetic self-correction examples (gradient training; data size not in packet).
setup: Gemma-2 2B, 9B and 27B; Llama-3.1-8B; Llama-3.3-70B; 38 'explain how' prompts; about 4,500-4,950 responses per model (Figure 2 caption).
numbers: Abstract: 'Llama-3.3-70B exhibits explicit ESR at 3.8%'; smaller models from the Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families show the explicit form less frequently (Figure 2: all below 1%).
Abstract: 'zero-ablating them reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%' for the 26 identified latents.
Contributions item 4: meta-prompting raises the multi-attempt rate; 'Llama-3.3-70B shows a 4.3× increase in multi-attempt rate (from 7.4% to 31.7%)' (Sec 4 text, Results).
limits: The metric counts only explicit verbal restarts; implicit recovery is not captured (per the authors).
Cannot disentangle scale, architecture and training as the cause of the gap between Llama-3.3-70B and smaller models (contributions item 1).
evidence_quote: and ablation (26 self-correction-associated latents clamped to zero; 4,875 trials) conditions.

title: Understanding Unreliability of Steering Vectors in Language Models: Geometric Predictors and the Limits of Linear Approximations
venue: Master's thesis, Eberhard Karls University of Tübingen (submitted June 2025; arXiv Feb 2026)
question: Why does steering reliability differ across behaviours, and what geometry of the training data predicts it?
mechanism: CAA steering vector from the mean of training activation differences. Diagnostics: (i) directional agreement, the cosine between each training activation difference and the steering vector; (ii) separability of positive and negative activations along the difference-of-means line, quantified by a discriminability index; (iii) separability along the first LDA component and along a logistic-regression direction, used as diagnostics; (iv) convergence of the steering vector across subsamples. Results are correlations of these predictors with per-dataset steerability rank.
training: none for the steering vector; logistic-regression and LDA fits are used as analysis tools on activation data, not as steering directions.
setup: MWE datasets (thesis Sec 4.1 and App. C.1); CAA; model and layer details are not captured from the packet.
numbers: Thesis abstract: 'higher cosine similarity between training activation differences predicts more reliable steering'; datasets whose positive and negative activations are better separated along the steering direction 'are more reliably steerable' (no numeric values in abstract; correlation tables are in Ch. 5 and were not captured).
limits: Steering vectors are unreliable when the latent target representation is not effectively approximated by the linear steering direction (abstract).
The thesis treats the linear-direction assumption itself as a limit (Ch. 2.4.4 and Ch. 6.3).
evidence_quote: First, I find that higher cosine similarity between training activation differences predicts more reliable steering.

novelty_note.C: Uses LDA and a logistic-regression direction as separability diagnostics on activation differences to predict steering reliability; these discriminant directions are measurement tools here, not the steering direction or a gate.

title: What Drives Representation Steering? A Mechanistic Case Study on Steering Refusal
question: Through which model components (attention OV vs QK circuits, MLPs) does a refusal steering vector act, and can the vector be sparsified?
mechanism: Refusal steering: difference of mean activations on harmful versus harmless instructions (following Arditi et al.), added as alpha * s at every token position including the prompt. Multi-token activation patching extended to steered generation; edges scored with EAP-IG (edge attribution patching with integrated gradients) by their indirect effect on the steered output. Steering value vector decomposition: the steering vector's contribution through the OV circuit is decomposed per dimension and interpreted. Sparsification keeps the most important dimensions of the steering vector (selection rule not captured from packet).
training: none for the steering vector (difference of means); EAP-IG uses gradients for attribution only.
setup: Gemma 2 2B Instruct, Llama 3.2 3B Instruct and Qwen 3 8B (non-thinking); harmful training data from AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct, TDC2023 and HarmBench; 100 JailbreakBench harmful and 100 Alpaca harmless test prompts.
numbers: Abstract: 'Freezing all attention scores during steering drops performance by only 8.83% across three model families.'
Abstract: steering vectors 'can be sparsified by up to 85-96% while retaining most performance'.
Contributions item 1: different steering methodologies 'leverage highly interchangeable circuits (≳ 90% overlap)'.
limits: interp: analysis is limited to refusal steering on three models; generality to other behaviours is not tested in the packet.
evidence_quote: indicating that the refusal vector largely ignores the QK circuit

title: A Geometric Account of Activation Steering through Angle-Norm Decomposition
question: Is concept information carried by the angle or the norm of a hidden state, and does the norm matter for steering stability?
mechanism: Decompose hidden state x = r u with u = c s + sqrt(1 - c^2) v, where r is the norm, s the concept direction, c the angular concept score and v the unit direction orthogonal to s. Six steering methods are compared in this framework. The main new one is spherical steering with norm scaling: y = beta r (gamma s + sqrt(1 - gamma^2) v), gamma the target concept score and beta a radial scale; beta = 1 reduces to norm-preserving spherical steering. Probes trained on normalised versus raw hidden states test where concept information lies.
training: Linear probes are trained on hidden states to test concept encoding; the interventions themselves are training-free.
setup: Seven language models from 1B to 70B parameters (including Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct); four concept datasets; evaluation by fold (Figure 2).
numbers: Contributions: 'modest norm increases can reduce perplexity by up to 1.8× without substantially changing the semantic steering effect'.
Figure 2 caption: 'At γ = 0.7, β = 1.2 achieves the lowest perplexity in all folds in our evaluation'.
limits: Concept information is primarily angular for the four datasets studied; the claim is for those concepts (Sec 1).
Strict norm preservation can cause large perplexity increases at high angular strength (Sec 1).
evidence_quote: and v is the unit residual direction orthogonal to s

title: Adversarial Robustness of Activation Steering in Large Language Models
question: Do steering vectors and the selected steering layer stay reliable when inference inputs are semantically preserved but adversarially perturbed?
mechanism: Four extraction methods (mean difference, PCA, ITI probes, ODESteer barrier function) produce a steering vector; three text-perturbation attack strategies are applied to test inputs; robustness is measured as directional robustness and strength reduction. Layer selection uses LayerNavigator's steerability score S_l = D_l + C_l (separability plus alignment of individual pairs with the global direction); the layer optimal on clean inputs is compared with the one optimal under perturbation. Extracting vectors from perturbed inputs is tested as a mitigation.
training: MD and PCA are training-free; ITI and ODESteer fit probes or barrier functions. The adversarial-training mitigation is described as adversarial training; its training details are not in the packet.
setup: Five models from 1.5B to 30B across two families; six persona datasets from Anthropic's Model-Written Evaluations.
numbers: Abstract: 'directional robustness drops by up to 64%'.
Abstract: under perturbation the optimal layer found by an automated method on clean inputs shifts 'by up to 17 positions under perturbation' (the abstract's wording).
limits: Extracting vectors from adversarially perturbed inputs partially recovers steerability for PCA and MD on mid-to-large models, but consistently fails to locate the improved optimal layer (abstract).
evidence_quote: Diamonds mark the layer selected by LayerNavigator. White Diamond marks when LayerNavigator selected layer matches the true optimal

title: On the Steering Dimensionality of Refusal in Language Models
venue: 40th NeurIPS 2026, Workshop: Interpretability as a Science (per header)
question: How many steering directions (the steering dimensionality) are needed to reliably induce and suppress refusal, and does this differ between safety-triggered and general refusal?
mechanism: Steering subspace V_k from a contrast matrix H of last-token activation differences: top-k PCA components, SVD right singular vectors, or K-means centroids. Additive steering: h' = h + V_k^T alpha_k with per-direction coefficients. Directional ablation: h' = (I - P_k) h, where P_k is the orthogonal projection onto the row space of V_k, written with the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse (eq. 2). A behaviour is t-dimensionally steerable when steering effect grows monotonically up to dimension t and saturates beyond it. Safety refusal contrast uses harmful versus harmless prompts; general refusal contrast instructs the model to write a refusing and an affirming response to the same harmless query.
training: none: PCA, SVD and K-means over contrast activations; the general-refusal contrast responses are generated by prompting the model.
setup: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (the two models named in the implementation details); 3 rollouts per input at temperature 0.6; Qwen3.8-27B used as judge, retaining 200 response pairs.
numbers: Abstract: refusal triggered by safety alignment is '1-dim steerable', while 'even 5-dim steering subspaces fail to reliably capture its full steerable variation' for general refusal.

Results: for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, steerability 'largely saturates beyond a 3-dim steering subspace using K-Means, yet directional ablation remains ineffective across all four evaluation settings' (general refusal).
limits: For Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, directional ablation 'substantially degrades response coherence' (Results); the authors read this as the subspace being entangled with general capabilities, which they say is undesirable.
evidence_quote: Although directional ablation can alter refusal behavior, it also substantially degrades response coherence.

novelty_note.D: For general refusal, the model is instructed to write a refusing response and an affirming response to the same harmless query, and these instruction-driven responses supply the contrast activations for the steering subspace.
novelty_note.E: Measures a dimensional capacity limit (the minimum number of directions one behaviour needs; a 5-dim subspace is insufficient for general refusal); this is per behaviour, not a prediction of interference between separate patches.
novelty_note.G: Reports that the extracted subspace for Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct degrades coherence, which the authors read as the steering signal being entangled with general capabilities rather than the refusal concept alone.

title: The Sharp Directions Are Against You: Curvature Analysis of Activation Steering
question: Why is CAA fragile (anti-steering on many inputs), and can removing the high-curvature part of the steering vector fix it without retraining?
mechanism: Steering Hessian H_steer = d^2 L / dv^2, where L is the next-token cross-entropy of a target token under the steered model, differentiated with respect to the steering vector v. Top-k eigenvectors by |lambda| form the sharp subspace S_k, estimated by Lanczos (m = 40 iterations, full reorthogonalisation) with Hessian-vector products from central finite differences over n = 12 prompts. Sharp removal: v_cleaned = v_CAA - P_{S_k} v_CAA. Proposition 2 bounds the direction change (cosine ≥ 1 - eps) and the curvature reduction kappa_gap = |lambda_1| / |lambda_{k+1}|; default k = 15.
training: none to the model: the Hessian is estimated by finite differences of gradients over a small prompt set (n = 12), and the correction is a one-off projection of the CAA vector.
setup: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B; four behavioural tasks; 36 token-level conditions (3 models x 4 tasks x 3 layers); open-ended generation over 25 conditions; refusal correction tested on Arditi et al.'s refusal direction (Sec 5.6).
numbers: Abstract: removing the sharp component 'approximately preserves its direction and magnitude (cosine > 0.974, norm reduction < 3% for typical settings) while reducing the vector's directional curvature by up to 12× (median 4× across 36 conditions)'.
Abstract: 'Sharp directions account for only 1–5% of the CAA vector's squared norm'; steering along them 'reverses the intended behavior in every condition tested, with anti-steer rates of 53–100%'.
Abstract: sharp removal 'outperforms standard CAA in open-ended generation across all 25 conditions tested'.
limits: Sharp removal is a post-processing step on the vector; the packet reports no inference-time cost beyond the one-off Hessian estimate.
Target-token robustness: the multi-token contrastive variant has cosine 0.61 with the single-token version (Sec 3.1).
evidence_quote: Removing the sharp component of a steering vector approximately preserves its direction and magnitude (cosine > 0.974, norm reduction < 3% for typical settings)

novelty_note.G: Argues the CAA vector's sharp-direction component acts as noise rather than signal: 'sharp directions act as noise rather than signal: they disrupt coherent behavioral control regardless of steering polarity' (abstract); CAA has the wrong sign on three of four tasks at most layers, so the vector's effect is driven by curvature rather than the intended concept.
